chunks.text: 3.1 Architecture overview HOCT is a two-stage Transformer (Fig. 1 d–e) whose attention layers encode spatial coordinates into queries and keys via 3D RoPE [ 48 ] with learnable per-head frequencies and a learnable reflection [ 33 ] . Node self-attention. Input features are projected to hidden dimension C C via 𝐳 i ( 0 ) = 𝐖 in ​ 𝐱 i \mathbf{z}_{i}^{(0)}=\mathbf{W}_{\mathrm{in}}\mathbf{x}_{i} , then refined through L n L_{n} self-attention layers. Each layer applies RoPE to queries and keys using the node position 𝐩 i \mathbf{p}_{i} , and masks out node pairs farther than a distance threshold τ \tau to preserve sparsity. Edge attention. For each candidate edge e = ( i , j ) e=(i,j) , we construct an edge token by concatenating the contextualized node features and projecting through an MLP: 𝐡 e ( 0 ) = MLP gather ⁡ ( [ 𝐳 i ( L n ) ∥ 𝐳 j ( L n ) ] ) \displaystyle\mathbf{h}_{e}^{(0)}=\operatorname{MLP}_{\mathrm{gather}}\bigl([\mathbf{z}_{i}^{(L_{n})}\|\mathbf{z}_{j}^{(L_{n})}]\bigr) (1) Where [ . ∥ . ] [.\|.] is the feature concatenation operator. The edge position for RoPE is the midpoint 𝐩 e = ( 𝐩 i + 𝐩 j ) / 2 \mathbf{p}_{e}=(\mathbf{p}_{i}+\mathbf{p}_{j})/2 . Edge tokens, 𝐡 e ( l ) \mathbf{h}_{e}^{(l)} , are then refined through L e L_{e} attention layers, with the first layer performing cross-attention with 𝐟 e \mathbf{f}_{e} as queries and 𝐡 e ( 0 ) \mathbf{h}_{e}^{(0)} as keys/values, grounding the edge representation in the raw feature relationships. Where 𝐟 e = 𝐖 edge ​ ( [ 𝐱 i ∥ 𝐱 j ] ) \mathbf{f}_{e}=\mathbf{W}_{\mathrm{edge}}([\mathbf{x}_{i}\|\mathbf{x}_{j}]) are the edge-features tokens computed from the raw input features. Subsequent layers perform self-attention among edge tokens. Every edge attention layer incorporates a geometric distance bias (Sec. 3.2 ) based on the line-to-line distance between edge pairs in addition to RoPE. Classification head.

The final edge embeddings are passed through LayerNorm and a linear projection to produce scalar logits ℓ e ∈ ℝ \ell_{e}\in\mathbb{R} , which are normalized via the parental softmax (Sec. 3.3 ). 4 Experiments 4.1 CTC benchmark Architecture and training. HOCT uses C = 288 C{=}288 , H = 4 H{=}4 heads, L n = L e = 4 L_{n}{=}L_{e}{=}4 layers, and distance threshold τ = 300 \tau{=}300 pixels. The model is trained on 16 datasets from the Cell Tracking Challenge (CTC) [ 36 ] , spanning brightfield, fluorescence, and phase-contrast microscopy in 2D and 3D. Each dataset contains two annotated time-lapse sequences (32 sequences total); we form two cross-validation splits by assigning one sequence per dataset to each split, training on one and evaluating on the other. Data augmentation includes spatial crops, affine transformations, and feature dropout that randomly zeroes entire feature groups to encourage robustness to missing features. Full training details (optimizer, schedule, augmentation, and ILP configuration) are in Appendix A . Metrics. We report standard CTC metrics [ 37 , 51 ] : LNK (Linking accuracy); BIO (Biological metric); and CLB (Cell Linking Benchmark), the main ranking metric for the challenge and the average between LNK and BIO; all in [ 0 , 1 ] [0,1] with higher being better. For the bacteria benchmark, we extract scores from [ 1 ] and report: AOGM (Acyclic Oriented Graph Metric, lower is better) with its decomposition into addition (AOGM-A) and deletion (AOGM-D) errors, and Division F1 . Topological label information. To quantify the non-homophilic claim from Sec. 1 , we build the line graph L ​ ( G C ) L(G_{C}) of each candidate tracking graph (where original edges become nodes that are connected when they share an endpoint) and measure label agreement on it; per-sequence statistics are in Appendix C .

Across the CTC sequences, the adjusted homophily [ 41 ] on L ​ ( G C ) L(G_{C}) is ℋ adj = 0.01 ± 0.04 \mathcal{H}_{\mathrm{adj}}=0.01\pm 0.04 , indistinguishable from random; for each true (GT) edge, only 29 % 29\% of its co-incident edges are also true, so 71 % 71\% of a correct link’s line-graph neighbors carry a conflicting label. For reference, standard homophilic benchmarks have ℋ adj > 0.5 \mathcal{H}_{\mathrm{adj}}>0.5 [ 41 ] , where graph neural networks succeed because topology carries the labels; candidate tracking graphs sit at the random baseline. This explains why GNN-based edge classification [ 2 ] has not surpassed simpler baselines: message passing aggregates over a topology that is uninformative by construction. 4.2 Ablations ILP solver components. 4.5 Incremental correction As a final experiment, to assess the argument that edge-embedding is a better paradigma, we evaluate how efficiently each system can be improved with limited user feedback [ 42 ] in an incremental correction setting on the three bacteria validation sequences from Sec. 4.4 . We compare against Attrackt [ 28 ] , which builds upon Trackastra, proposing an unsupervised pre-training for tracking and human-in-the-loop fine-tuning. Both HOCT and Trackastra + Attrackt [ 17 , 28 ] start from their respective CTC-pretrained weights (never trained on bacteria training data) and run 20 rounds of 20 annotations each (400 total). HOCT annotates candidate edges and refits a logistic regression head on frozen edge embeddings; Trackastra annotates nodes and, in its strongest variants developed exclusively for human-in-the-loop training [ 30 ] , it fine-tunes the network via LoRA [ 22 ] . A linear classifier head cannot be applied to Trackastra, because it encodes associations as dot-product similarity between node embeddings; the closest analogue is a linear probe that learns a single map L L applied to both embeddings before the dot product, replacing ⟨ 𝐧 i , 𝐧 j ⟩ \langle\mathbf{n}_{i},\mathbf{n}_{j}\rangle with ⟨ L ​ 𝐧 i , L ​ 𝐧 j ⟩ \langle L\mathbf{n}_{i},L\mathbf{n}_{j}\rangle , which we also include in the comparison. Each system uses multiple sampling strategies (Table 5 ); full details are in Appendix D . Results. Table 5 and Fig. 2 compare both systems across all strategies. HOCT starts from a better baseline (AOGM 1418 1418 vs. 4951 4951 ) and improves much more rapidly, which is unexpected as there is more room for improvement for Trackastra. The best HOCT strategy ( uncertainty ) reduces AOGM by 59 % 59\% after 400 annotations, while the best Trackastra+Attrackt strategy ( LoRA + unsup ) achieves only a 6.75 % 6.75\% reduction despite using LoRA fine-tuning with 2000 gradient steps per round.

The full HOCT round (logistic refit + inference + ILP + metrics on all three sequences) takes ∼ {\sim} 2 min, ILP-dominated and comparable to Trackastra’s frozen-model strategies – well within the latency budget for active learning, in contrast to the ∼ {\sim} 40–55 min per round required by LoRA fine-tuning. LoRA + unsup is the strongest Attrackt variant once its image autoencoder embeddings and MLP_E / MLP_D weights are pretrained on the validation data (Appendix D ); without that pretraining, the unsupervised reconstruction loss is numerically dominant and degrades performance. The linear probe (a single learned matrix applied to both embeddings before the dot product) reaches − 2.2 % -2.2\% , slightly above the frozen-model baselines but well below LoRA fine-tuning. Because the two systems start from very different baselines (HOCT: 1418; Trackastra: 4951), Fig. 2 normalizes each curve to its round-0 value. HOCT’s gains concentrate in the early rounds: the first 80 annotations account for roughly half the total reduction, and active strategies outperform random sampling. Trackastra + Attrackt curves remain near-flat: even LoRA + unsup, which updates ∼ 5 % {\sim}5\% of model weights per round, reinforcing that explicit per-edge features enable cheaper and more effective correction than implicit node-similarity representations. 4.2 Ablations ILP solver components. The Edge-Transformer baseline, which removes only the geometric biases of Sec. 3.2 while keeping global attention, also underperforms, isolating the contribution of line-to-line distance encoding from that of unrestricted attention. 5 Conclusion HOCT is an edge-centric Transformer that classifies candidate cell links via attention biased by inter-link geometry, addressing both the connected-manifold problem at divisions and the absence of topological label information in candidate tracking graphs.

With only simple geometric features and no pre-trained image encoder, it matches or surpasses prior methods across the Cell Tracking Challenge and a bacteria-division benchmark; a logistic head on frozen HOCT features further outperforms LoRA fine-tuning of a Trackastra baseline in a 400-annotation human-in-the-loop setting. Limitations. The edge-centric architecture comes at increased computational cost. While standard node-association Transformers have attention complexity O ​ ( | V | 2 ) O(|V|^{2}) , HOCT requires O ​ ( | E | 2 ) O(|E|^{2}) for the edge attention stage. We mitigate this by constraining the candidate graph to k k nearest neighbors per node, yielding O ​ ( | V | 2 ​ k 2 ) O(|V|^{2}k^{2}) . This is a significant increase in memory requirements (e.g. 100 × 100{\times} for k = 10 k{=}10 ), but manageable because the model is compact ( C = 288 C{=}288 , 2 × 4 2\times 4 layers) compared to architectures in other domains. The spatial distance mask further reduces the effective number of attended pairs. Extending to very large fields of view with thousands of cells per frame requires tiling, as is currently done when applying image-based models to large microscopy datasets. Broader impact. Accurate cell tracking advances biological research by enabling quantitative analysis of cell behavior in development, regeneration, and disease models. Potential downstream applications include drug screening, cancer-metastasis assays, and developmental-biology studies. As with other biological tools, there is a risk of misuse in unethical research contexts, though we expect the primary impact to be beneficial.
